statement: In an advert, a big smile makes a person look happy.
explanation: A smile is the clearest sign of happiness in a picture.

statement: A person who is crying looks happy.
explanation: Crying shows that a person is sad or upset.

statement: Red, yellow and orange are warm colours.
explanation: They remind us of fire and the sun, so we call them warm.

statement: Blue and grey are warm colours.
explanation: Blue and grey are cold colours. Red, orange and yellow are warm.

statement: A dark picture has very little light in it.
explanation: Dark means there is not much light.

statement: A bright picture has very little light in it.
explanation: A bright picture has a lot of light.

statement: A poster is a large printed picture with words, put up for people to see.
explanation: Posters are put on walls to show or sell something.

statement: An advert is made to stop people from buying a product.
explanation: An advert is made to make people want to buy something.

statement: A close-up shows a face or a small detail.
explanation: The camera is very near, so the face or object fills the picture.

statement: A close-up shows a big field from very far away.
explanation: A shot from far away is a long shot. A close-up is very near.

statement: A busy picture has lots of things in it.
explanation: Busy means full of people, objects or movement.

statement: An empty room is full of people and things.
explanation: An empty room has nothing, or almost nothing, in it.

statement: Fast, loud music makes an advert feel more exciting.
explanation: Fast, loud music gives an advert energy.

statement: Slow, quiet music makes a scene feel fast and exciting.
explanation: Slow, quiet music makes a scene feel calm.

statement: A colourful picture has many different colours.
explanation: Colourful means full of colours.

statement: A black and white photo is very colourful.
explanation: A black and white photo has no colours, only black, white and grey.

statement: On most magazine covers, the name of the magazine is at the top.
explanation: The name at the top helps people find the magazine in a shop.

statement: A scary film poster normally uses soft pink colours and smiling faces.
explanation: Scary film posters use dark colours, shadows and frightened faces.

statement: A frown shows that a person is unhappy, angry or worried.
explanation: When we frown, we pull our eyebrows down and together.

statement: A person with their arms in the air and a big smile looks sad.
explanation: Arms in the air and a big smile show that the person is happy or excited.

statement: A funny advert tries to make people laugh.
explanation: Funny means it makes you laugh.

statement: A serious news report tries to make people laugh at the news.
explanation: A serious report gives information in a calm, sensible way.

statement: The words on a poster help us understand the picture.
explanation: The words tell us what the picture is about.

statement: A photo of a sunny beach looks cold and dark.
explanation: A sunny beach looks warm and bright.

statement: Snow and ice in a picture make it look cold.
explanation: We connect snow and ice with cold weather.

statement: A crowded street has very few people in it.
explanation: A crowded street has a lot of people in it.

statement: A calm sea has small, gentle waves.
explanation: Calm means quiet and still, with no big waves.

statement: A friendly person in an advert looks cross and turns away from us.
explanation: A friendly person smiles and looks at us.

statement: Soft, warm light makes a room look cosy.
explanation: Warm light, like from a lamp or a fire, feels comfortable.

statement: A new phone in an advert looks old, dirty and broken.
explanation: Adverts show new products as clean, shiny and perfect.

statement: A photo is a picture taken with a camera.
explanation: Photo is short for photograph.

statement: A cartoon is a photo of real people.
explanation: A cartoon is drawn, not photographed.

statement: Big, bold letters are easy to see from far away.
explanation: That is why posters and signs use big, bold letters.

statement: In a film, a whisper is a very loud way of speaking.
explanation: A whisper is very quiet. It can make a scene feel secret or tense.

statement: Scary film posters use a lot of dark colours and shadows.
explanation: Darkness and shadows make us feel afraid.

statement: Happy birthday cards are usually printed in black and grey.
explanation: Birthday cards use bright, cheerful colours.

statement: A clean, white kitchen in an advert looks fresh and tidy.
explanation: White and clean things look new and fresh.

statement: A strong person in a picture looks weak and tired.
explanation: A strong person looks powerful and full of energy.

statement: A boring picture does not make people want to look at it for long.
explanation: Boring means not interesting.

statement: An exciting advert is slow and quiet, with very little happening.
explanation: An exciting advert is full of action, colour and energy.

statement: Green makes us think of nature because grass and trees are green.
explanation: That is why green is used for nature and the environment.

statement: Red is the colour most used to show calm and sleep.
explanation: Red is used for danger, love and excitement. Soft blue is used for calm.

statement: In a photo, people far away look smaller than people near the camera.
explanation: Things look smaller the further away they are.

statement: A thumbs-up shows that a person is unhappy.
explanation: A thumbs-up shows that a person is happy or agrees.

statement: A sad song makes a scene feel sadder.
explanation: Music changes how we feel about what we see.

statement: A cheerful character looks grumpy and miserable.
explanation: A cheerful character looks happy and bright.

statement: A familiar face is a face that people know.
explanation: Familiar means known or seen before.

statement: A strange place is a place that you know very well.
explanation: A strange place is new, unusual or unknown.

statement: A fake smile is a smile that is not real.
explanation: Fake means not real.

statement: A quiet scene has lots of loud noise.
explanation: A quiet scene has little or no noise.

statement: A low-angle shot looks up at a person and makes them seem more powerful.
explanation: Looking up at someone makes them look big and important.

statement: A high-angle shot looks up at a person and makes them seem powerful.
explanation: A high-angle shot looks down, so the person looks small or weak.

statement: A long shot shows a person's whole body and some of the place around them.
explanation: It helps us see who the person is and where they are.

statement: A long shot is filmed very close to a person's eyes.
explanation: A shot of just the eyes is an extreme close-up.

statement: The masthead is the magazine's name on its front cover.
explanation: It is in large letters so readers can find the magazine.

statement: Cover lines are the page numbers at the bottom of a magazine page.
explanation: Cover lines are the short headlines on the cover about stories inside.

statement: A slogan is a short, memorable phrase used in advertising.
explanation: For example, Nike's 'Just do it'.

statement: A logo is a long paragraph that explains a product.
explanation: A logo is a small symbol or design that shows who made the product.

statement: A glossy magazine has shiny paper and high-quality photos.
explanation: Glossy means smooth and shiny.

statement: A faded photo has very strong, bright colours.
explanation: A faded photo has pale, weak colours, often because it is old.

statement: A persuasive advert tries to make you do something, such as buy a product.
explanation: Persuade means to make someone believe or do something.

statement: An informative leaflet is mainly designed to make people laugh.
explanation: An informative leaflet gives facts and information.

statement: Direct address is when a person in an image looks straight at the audience.
explanation: It feels as if they are speaking to you.

statement: A close-up of a product is used to hide it from the audience.
explanation: A close-up shows the product in detail.

statement: Glamorous people in adverts wear expensive-looking clothes, make-up and jewellery.
explanation: Glamour is about luxury and beauty.

statement: A realistic advert shows a world of dragons and magic.
explanation: A realistic advert shows ordinary life as it really is.

statement: A balanced layout has a similar amount of text and images on each side.
explanation: This makes the page look calm and organised.

statement: A spacious room is small and full of furniture.
explanation: A spacious room is big, with lots of space.

statement: Lighting a face from below makes a person look scary, as in horror films.
explanation: Light from below throws strange shadows up the face.

statement: Soft, bright lighting is used to make heroes in adverts look frightening.
explanation: Soft, bright lighting makes people look friendly and attractive.

statement: The target audience is the group of people a media text is made for.
explanation: For example, a skateboard magazine is aimed at young skaters.

statement: The target audience is the company that pays for an advert.
explanation: That company is the advertiser. The target audience is who the advert is for.

statement: An upbeat song has a fast, happy feel.
explanation: Upbeat means cheerful and positive.

statement: A tense scene makes the audience feel relaxed and sleepy.
explanation: A tense scene makes the audience feel nervous and worried.

statement: Exaggerated features, like a huge smile or giant eyes, are common in cartoons.
explanation: Exaggeration makes characters funny and easy to read.

statement: A predictable story is full of surprises.
explanation: A predictable story is easy to guess. It has few surprises.

statement: Repetitive music repeats the same sounds again and again.
explanation: Repetitive means repeating.

statement: In Western adverts, a traditional wedding dress is usually bright green.
explanation: A traditional Western wedding dress is white.

statement: A youthful image makes a person or product look young and fresh.
explanation: Youthful means young or looking young.

statement: A modern design looks old-fashioned, as if it was made a hundred years ago.
explanation: A modern design looks new and up to date.

statement: Body language is the message we send with our body, such as how we stand or sit.
explanation: Crossed arms, for example, can look unfriendly.

statement: Facial expression means the clothes a person is wearing.
explanation: Facial expression is what the face shows, such as a smile or a frown. Clothes are costume.

statement: Costume means the clothes and accessories a character wears.
explanation: Costume tells us about a character's job, age or personality.

statement: A prop is the background music in a film.
explanation: A prop is an object that a character uses or holds.

statement: The setting is the place and time where a scene happens.
explanation: For example, a dark forest at night.

statement: A headline is the small print at the very end of a newspaper article.
explanation: A headline is the big title at the top of an article.

statement: A caption is a short piece of text that goes with a photo.
explanation: It tells us who or what is in the photo.

statement: An attention-grabbing headline is small, grey and hard to notice.
explanation: An attention-grabbing headline is big and bold, so you notice it at once.

statement: Red text on a poster is used to grab attention.
explanation: Red is a strong colour that the eye notices quickly.

statement: Sad, slow music is the usual choice for an advert selling a fun holiday.
explanation: Holiday adverts use happy, upbeat music.

statement: An ordinary person in an advert looks like an everyday member of the public, not a star.
explanation: Ordinary people make an advert feel relatable.

statement: A natural look in a photo means lots of heavy make-up and editing.
explanation: A natural look means little make-up or editing.

statement: Dramatic music and lighting make a scene feel more exciting or serious.
explanation: They tell the audience that something important is happening.

statement: A memorable slogan is one that people forget quickly.
explanation: A memorable slogan is easy to remember.

statement: An accessible website is easy for everyone to use, including disabled people.
explanation: Accessible means easy to reach, use or understand.

statement: An effective advert is one that fails to get its message across.
explanation: An effective advert works: it gets its message across.

statement: A static image does not move.
explanation: Static means still. A photo is a static image.

statement: A static shot is one where the camera moves around very fast.
explanation: In a static shot the camera stays still.

statement: A reassuring voice-over sounds calm and confident.
explanation: Reassuring means making people feel safe and less worried.

statement: A gentle character in a film shouts and hits people.
explanation: A gentle character is kind, calm and careful.

statement: Representation is the way people, places or ideas are shown in the media.
explanation: Every representation is chosen and constructed by someone.

statement: A stereotype is a detailed picture of one real, individual person.
explanation: A stereotype is a simple, fixed idea about a whole group.

statement: Mise-en-scène means everything placed in front of the camera, including setting, costume, props and lighting.
explanation: It is French for 'putting in the scene'.

statement: Mise-en-scène is the music that is added after filming.
explanation: Mise-en-scène is what we see in the frame. Music is part of the sound.

statement: Denotation is what we literally see in an image.
explanation: For example: a red rose.

statement: Connotation is the literal, surface meaning of an image.
explanation: That is denotation. Connotation is the idea or feeling it suggests, such as love.

statement: In adverts, a red rose connotes love or romance.
explanation: This meaning comes from culture, especially Valentine's Day.

statement: A white dove is a common symbol of war.
explanation: A white dove is a symbol of peace.

statement: Muted colours are soft and less bright.
explanation: Muted colours feel calm, serious or old-fashioned.

statement: Vibrant colours are dull and faded.
explanation: Vibrant colours are bright and full of energy.

statement: A grainy image looks rough and less sharp, like an old film or a cheap camera.
explanation: Grain can make an image feel real, old or secret.

statement: A minimalist poster is full of text, pictures and decoration.
explanation: A minimalist poster uses very few elements and lots of empty space.

statement: A cluttered layout has a lot of items crowded together.
explanation: Cluttered layouts can feel busy or messy.

statement: An idealised image shows people exactly as they are, with all their flaws.
explanation: An idealised image shows people as more perfect than they really are.

statement: Airbrushing removes marks and wrinkles to make skin look perfect.
explanation: It is a common way of idealising models in magazines.

statement: Aspirational adverts show lives that the audience would not want.
explanation: Aspirational adverts show a life the audience dreams of having.

statement: An inclusive advert shows people of different ages, ethnicities and abilities.
explanation: Inclusive means including people who are often left out.

statement: A diverse cast is made up of people who look very similar.
explanation: A diverse cast includes people of many different backgrounds.

statement: Sepia tones give a photo a brown, old-fashioned look that feels nostalgic.
explanation: Sepia reminds us of very old photographs.

statement: A nostalgic advert focuses on the future and new technology.
explanation: A nostalgic advert looks back fondly at the past.

statement: In Western culture, black is a traditional colour of mourning.
explanation: People wear black to funerals.

statement: On road signs, green is the traditional colour of danger.
explanation: Red and yellow are used for danger. Green usually means safe or go.

statement: Cross-cutting moves between two scenes that are happening at the same time.
explanation: It builds tension, for example in a chase.

statement: A slow-motion shot shows action faster than in real life.
explanation: Slow motion shows action more slowly than in real life.

statement: A two-shot shows two people in the same frame.
explanation: It shows the relationship between them.

statement: An over-the-shoulder shot is filmed from directly above the characters.
explanation: Over-the-shoulder is filmed from behind one person. Directly above is a bird's-eye view.

statement: A bird's-eye view shot looks straight down from above.
explanation: It makes people look small and the place look big.

statement: A point-of-view shot shows a character from far away, so we see the whole room.
explanation: A point-of-view shot shows what a character sees, through their eyes.

statement: A canted angle tilts the camera to make a scene feel uneasy.
explanation: It is also called a Dutch angle.

statement: High-key lighting creates strong, dark shadows, as in horror films.
explanation: High-key lighting is bright, with few shadows. Low-key lighting has strong shadows.

statement: Low-key lighting uses a lot of shadow and is common in horror and crime films.
explanation: Shadows create mystery and fear.

statement: The stereotypical scientist in films is a young woman in casual clothes.
explanation: The stereotype is an older man in a white coat and glasses.

statement: The 'damsel in distress' is a stereotype of a helpless woman who needs to be rescued.
explanation: She waits for a man to save her.

statement: A counter-stereotype is an image that matches the usual stereotype exactly.
explanation: A counter-stereotype goes against the usual stereotype.

statement: Showing a man as a caring stay-at-home dad goes against a traditional gender stereotype.
explanation: Traditionally, women were shown as the main carers.

statement: Authentic images are staged and heavily edited to look perfect.
explanation: Authentic images look real and natural, not staged or edited.

statement: A credible news source is one that people trust to tell the truth.
explanation: Credible means believable.

statement: A misleading headline gives readers an accurate and fair picture of the story.
explanation: A misleading headline gives a false or wrong idea.

statement: The rule of thirds divides an image into nine equal parts with two horizontal and two vertical lines.
explanation: Important things are placed on the lines or where they cross.

statement: The rule of thirds says the main subject belongs in the exact centre of the frame.
explanation: It places the subject on a third line, away from the centre.

statement: A suspenseful scene makes the audience anxious to know what happens next.
explanation: Suspense keeps us watching.

statement: Atmospheric lighting and sound have no effect on the mood of a scene.
explanation: They create the mood of a scene.

statement: Non-diegetic sound, such as a film's soundtrack, cannot be heard by the characters.
explanation: It is added for the audience only.

statement: Diegetic sound comes from outside the world of the story, like a narrator's voice.
explanation: That is non-diegetic sound. Diegetic sound comes from inside the story, like dialogue.

statement: A sentimental advert aims to make the audience feel tender emotions, such as love or sadness.
explanation: Christmas adverts are often sentimental.

statement: An intimate shot places the audience far away from the characters.
explanation: An intimate shot brings the audience close, often with a close-up.

statement: Consistent branding uses the same colours, fonts and logo across different adverts.
explanation: This makes the brand easy to recognise.

statement: A distinctive design looks the same as the other products on the shelf.
explanation: A distinctive design stands out and is easy to recognise.

statement: A tagline is a short phrase on a poster that sums up the film or product.
explanation: For example: 'In space no one can hear you scream' (Alien).

statement: On a film poster, the billing block is the large main image of the star.
explanation: The billing block is the small block of credits at the bottom of the poster.

statement: Anchorage is when text, such as a caption, fixes the meaning of an image.
explanation: The words tell the audience how to read the picture.

statement: Anchorage means leaving an image open to many different meanings.
explanation: Anchorage narrows the meaning down. An image left open is polysemic.

statement: Roland Barthes wrote about denotation and connotation in images.
explanation: He was a French theorist of semiotics, the study of signs.

statement: The term 'male gaze' was introduced by Roland Barthes.
explanation: It was introduced by Laura Mulvey.

statement: Laura Mulvey introduced the idea of the 'male gaze' in a 1975 essay about cinema.
explanation: The essay is 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema'.

statement: The male gaze describes women being filmed as active heroes who drive the story.
explanation: The male gaze shows women as objects to be looked at, from a man's point of view.

statement: Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding model describes preferred, negotiated and oppositional readings.
explanation: Audiences can accept, partly accept or reject a text's message.

statement: An oppositional reading is when the audience fully accepts the message the producer intended.
explanation: That is a preferred reading. An oppositional reading rejects the message.

statement: Claude Lévi-Strauss is linked with the idea of binary oppositions, such as good versus evil.
explanation: Meaning comes from pairs of opposites.

statement: Binary oppositions are pairs of ideas that mean the same thing.
explanation: They are pairs of opposites, such as hero and villain.

statement: Vladimir Propp identified character types such as the hero, the villain and the helper in folk tales.
explanation: He studied Russian folk tales.

statement: Todorov's theory is about character types such as the hero, the villain and the donor.
explanation: Those are Propp's character types. Todorov's theory is about narrative structure.

statement: Todorov's narrative theory moves from equilibrium to disruption to a new equilibrium.
explanation: Equilibrium means a state of balance.

statement: A mode of address is the postal address printed on a magazine.
explanation: A mode of address is the way a text speaks to its audience.

statement: A magazine that uses 'you', slang and a chatty tone has an informal mode of address.
explanation: It talks to readers like a friend.

statement: A saturated image has weak, pale colours.
explanation: A saturated image has strong, intense colours.

statement: An asymmetrical composition is not the same on both sides.
explanation: Asymmetry can make an image feel dynamic or unsettling.

statement: A subtle message is loud, obvious and hard to miss.
explanation: A subtle message is quiet and easy to miss.

statement: An ambiguous image has more than one possible meaning.
explanation: Ambiguity makes audiences think or argue about the meaning.

statement: Irony is when what is said or shown matches exactly what is meant.
explanation: Irony is when the real meaning is different from, or the opposite of, what is said or shown.

statement: Emotive language is chosen to make the audience feel strong emotions.
explanation: For example: 'heartbreaking', 'shocking', 'tragic'.

statement: A selective representation includes the whole story of a person or event.
explanation: A selective representation chooses some parts and leaves others out.

statement: Stylised images exaggerate or simplify reality for effect.
explanation: Animation and fashion photography are often stylised.

statement: Naturalistic acting is deliberately exaggerated, like theatre for a large audience.
explanation: Naturalistic acting looks like real life. Exaggerated acting is theatrical.

statement: Hegemony is the idea that a dominant group's values come to seem like common sense.
explanation: The idea comes from Antonio Gramsci.

statement: Ferdinand de Saussure is best known for the theory of hegemony.
explanation: Hegemony is Antonio Gramsci's idea. Saussure is known for the signifier and the signified.

statement: Ferdinand de Saussure described a sign as a signifier plus a signified.
explanation: The signifier is the form; the signified is the idea.

statement: In semiotics, the 'signified' is the physical form of a sign, such as a word or picture.
explanation: That is the signifier. The signified is the idea or concept.

statement: Charles Peirce divided signs into icons, indexes and symbols.
explanation: An icon looks like what it means; an index is linked by cause; a symbol is a learned convention.

statement: A photograph of a cat is a symbol of a cat because it does not look like one.
explanation: A photo looks like its subject, so it is an icon.

statement: Smoke is an index of fire because it is directly caused by it.
explanation: An index points to its cause.

statement: A red traffic light means 'stop' because it naturally looks like stopping.
explanation: It is a symbol: its meaning is a learned convention.

statement: Erving Goffman studied how men and women are posed in adverts in his book 'Gender Advertisements'.
explanation: It was published in 1979.

statement: Goffman found that adverts usually show women as taller and more powerful than men.
explanation: Goffman found that men were usually shown as larger and higher than women.

statement: Goffman's 'feminine touch' describes women in adverts lightly touching objects or themselves.
explanation: It suggests delicacy rather than strength.

statement: Cultivation theory says that one short advert changes a viewer's beliefs straight away.
explanation: Cultivation theory is about the slow effect of heavy viewing over a long time.

statement: George Gerbner's cultivation theory says heavy TV viewing shapes how people see the real world over time.
explanation: Heavy viewers may see the world as more dangerous than it is.

statement: In Hall's model, a negotiated reading means rejecting a text's message outright.
explanation: A negotiated reading accepts part of the message and rejects or changes the rest.

statement: Uses and gratifications theory says audiences choose media to meet needs such as entertainment and information.
explanation: It is linked with Blumler and Katz.

statement: Blumler and Katz are best known for the hypodermic needle model.
explanation: Blumler and Katz are linked with uses and gratifications theory.

statement: The hypodermic needle model suggests media messages are 'injected' straight into a passive audience.
explanation: It is an early and now widely criticised theory.

statement: A manipulative advert gives viewers a fair, balanced view of a product.
explanation: A manipulative advert controls or tricks the viewer's feelings.

statement: A theatrical performance in a film is big and exaggerated, as if on a stage.
explanation: Theatrical means like the theatre.

statement: Contrived scenes look natural and unplanned.
explanation: Contrived scenes look forced and artificial.

statement: Derivative work copies or closely imitates earlier work.
explanation: It is the opposite of original.

statement: An innovative design repeats ideas that have been used many times before.
explanation: An innovative design introduces new ideas.

statement: A jump cut is an abrupt cut that makes time seem to jump forward.
explanation: It is common in vlogs and music videos.

statement: A match cut joins two shots that look and move very differently.
explanation: A match cut joins two shots that share a similar shape, movement or sound.

statement: A sombre advert uses dark tones and a serious mood.
explanation: Sombre means dark and serious.

statement: Immersive media keeps the audience at a distance, as outside observers.
explanation: Immersive media makes the audience feel inside the experience.

statement: In 'Mythologies' (1957), Roland Barthes analysed everyday images and objects as carriers of myth.
explanation: For Barthes, myth makes cultural values look natural.

statement: Barthes's enigma code refers to actions that tell the audience what will happen next.
explanation: That is the action code. The enigma code creates questions the audience wants answered.

statement: Barthes's action code refers to actions that suggest what will happen next in a narrative.
explanation: For example, a character loading a gun.

statement: Stuart Hall's encoding/decoding model treats audiences as passive receivers with a single possible reading.
explanation: Hall argued audiences can read a text in different ways: preferred, negotiated or oppositional.

statement: Stuart Hall argued that representation does not simply reflect reality but constructs meaning.
explanation: Meaning is produced through language and images.

statement: Laura Mulvey's 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema' is mainly about social class in advertising.
explanation: It is about gender and the male gaze in film.

statement: Mulvey drew on psychoanalysis, including Freud and Lacan, in her theory of the male gaze.
explanation: She called psychoanalysis a 'political weapon'.

statement: bell hooks's 'oppositional gaze' describes Black spectators fully accepting dominant images of themselves.
explanation: The oppositional gaze is a critical, resisting way of looking back at those images.

statement: bell hooks wrote her name in lower case to put the focus on her ideas rather than on herself.
explanation: Her real name was Gloria Jean Watkins.

statement: Judith Butler is best known for the theory of hyperreality.
explanation: Hyperreality is Jean Baudrillard's idea. Butler is known for gender performativity.

statement: Judith Butler's theory of gender performativity says gender is constructed through repeated acts.
explanation: It comes from her book 'Gender Trouble' (1990).

statement: David Gauntlett's identity theory is based on the Bobo doll experiments.
explanation: The Bobo doll experiments were Albert Bandura's. Gauntlett writes about media and identity.

statement: David Gauntlett argues that the media offer 'tools' that people use to think about their own identities.
explanation: Audiences pick and mix from what they see.

statement: Liesbet van Zoonen is best known for the encoding/decoding model.
explanation: The encoding/decoding model is Stuart Hall's. Van Zoonen is a feminist media theorist.

statement: Liesbet van Zoonen argued that the meaning of gender varies according to cultural and historical context.
explanation: Gender is a discourse, not a fixed fact.

statement: Paul Gilroy's 'The Black Atlantic' argues that Black identity is tied to one single nation.
explanation: Gilroy describes a transnational Black culture formed across the Atlantic.

statement: Edward Said's 'Orientalism' criticises Western representations of the 'East' as exotic and inferior.
explanation: It was published in 1978.

statement: Edward Said's 'Orientalism' is a study of how Eastern cultures represented the West.
explanation: It is about how the West represented the East.

statement: In Propp's theory, the dispatcher is the character who sends the hero on their quest.
explanation: The donor is different: the donor gives the hero something that helps.

statement: Richard Dyer's star theory says film stars have no constructed image.
explanation: Dyer argues that a star's image is carefully constructed across films, interviews and publicity.

statement: Tessa Perkins argued that stereotypes are not always negative or entirely false.
explanation: Her essay is 'Rethinking Stereotypes' (1979).

statement: Jean Baudrillard's 'hyperreality' describes media images that are perfect copies of an original reality.
explanation: Hyperreality is when simulations replace reality and seem more real than the real.

statement: Baudrillard used the term 'simulacra' for copies that have no original.
explanation: It comes from 'Simulacra and Simulation' (1981).

statement: Antonio Gramsci was a French semiotician who studied advertising images.
explanation: Gramsci was an Italian Marxist thinker, known for the idea of hegemony.

statement: Gramsci described hegemony as power maintained largely through consent rather than force.
explanation: Dominant values come to seem like common sense.

statement: Steve Neale's best-known work is about the representation of ethnicity in the news.
explanation: Neale is best known for his work on film genre.

statement: Steve Neale described genre in terms of repetition and difference.
explanation: Familiar elements are repeated, with something new each time.

statement: 'The medium is the message' is a phrase from Roland Barthes's 'Mythologies'.
explanation: The phrase is Marshall McLuhan's, from 'Understanding Media' (1964).

statement: McLuhan's 'the medium is the message' suggests that the form of a medium shapes society as much as its content.
explanation: It comes from 'Understanding Media' (1964).

statement: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment suggested that children ignore violent behaviour they watch.
explanation: Children who watched an adult hit the doll copied the behaviour.

statement: Albert Bandura's Bobo doll experiments are linked to social learning theory.
explanation: We learn by watching and copying others.

statement: The Bechdel test was created by the film director Steven Spielberg.
explanation: It comes from a comic strip by the cartoonist Alison Bechdel.

statement: The Bechdel test asks whether a film has two women who talk to each other about something other than a man.
explanation: It comes from a 1985 comic strip by Alison Bechdel.

statement: A hegemonic representation challenges the values of the dominant group.
explanation: A hegemonic representation supports the dominant values.

statement: A subversive representation challenges or undermines conventional values.
explanation: For example, a fairy tale where the princess rescues the prince.

statement: Voyeuristic camerawork makes the spectator feel watched, rather than watching.
explanation: Voyeuristic camerawork puts the spectator in the position of secretly watching someone.

statement: Intertextuality is when a media text refers to or borrows from another text.
explanation: For example, an advert that copies a famous film scene.

statement: A self-referential advert avoids any acknowledgement that it is an advert.
explanation: A self-referential advert openly draws attention to itself as an advert.

statement: An archetypal character embodies a universal type, such as the wise mentor.
explanation: Archetypes appear across many cultures and stories.

statement: An allegorical film has a literal meaning and no hidden one.
explanation: An allegory has a second, hidden meaning, often political or moral.

statement: Satire uses humour, irony or exaggeration to criticise people or institutions.
explanation: For example, a cartoon mocking a politician.

statement: A didactic text avoids teaching the audience anything.
explanation: A didactic text sets out to teach or give a moral lesson.

statement: A nonlinear narrative presents events out of chronological order.
explanation: For example, through flashbacks.

statement: Elliptical editing shows each moment of an action in real time.
explanation: Elliptical editing leaves out parts of an action to save time.

statement: An anachronism is something placed in the wrong historical period, such as a smartphone in a medieval drama.
explanation: Ana- means against; chronos means time.

statement: Reductive representations show the full complexity of a group of people.
explanation: Reductive representations simplify a group too much.

statement: Postcolonial theory examines how media representations are shaped by the history of empire.
explanation: Edward Said and Paul Gilroy are two postcolonial theorists.

statement: Barthes argued that a caption usually opens an image up to more meanings.
explanation: Barthes called this anchorage: a caption narrows the meaning down.

statement: A polysemic image is open to several different readings.
explanation: Anchorage, such as a caption, can narrow the meaning down.

statement: In Propp's theory, the false hero is the character who helps the hero most.
explanation: The false hero pretends to be the hero and tries to take the credit.
